title: The Student Pitch Where Klarna's Founders Came Last of Three
dek: Around 2005 a jury of Sweden's business elite dismissed three students' plan to let shoppers pay after delivery; the founders gave themselves six months to find out.

story.founder: Sebastian Siemiatkowski, Niklas Adalberth, Victor Jacobsson
story.event: Finishing last in the Stockholm School of Economics entrepreneurship competition and carrying on
story.summary: Around 2004-05, Sebastian Siemiatkowski, Niklas Adalberth and Victor Jacobsson pitched Kreditor, a pay-after-delivery service for online shops, at the Stockholm School of Economics entrepreneurship competition; by the founders' account a jury of senior Swedish business figures was unconvinced and the team ranked last of three. They gave themselves six months to make it work, took about 600,000 kronor from angel investor Jane Walerud for 10 per cent, and signed up small web shops across Sweden; the company was renamed Klarna in 2009.
paragraphs: The judges were some of the most powerful people in Swedish business. At the Stockholm School of Economics' annual entrepreneurship competition, three students, Sebastian Siemiatkowski, Niklas Adalberth and Victor Jacobsson, pitched Kreditor, a company that would let people shopping online pay after their goods arrived. By Siemiatkowski's account the jury included H&M's chairman, Stefan Persson, and a member of the Wallenberg family, and Sweden's king was in the audience. Swedish reports put the contest in 2004 or 2005.

The idea had come out of a gap year gone wrong. Siemiatkowski and Adalberth, friends since working at Burger King as teenagers, had hitchhiked round the world without flying and come home to find they had missed the deadline to re-register for classes. Living on welfare, Siemiatkowski took a sales job at a factoring company and saw small web shops insisting on payment upfront from wary customers. Swedes were used to paying for mail orders on delivery, and he began to wonder whether the same could work online.

"Unfortunately, none of them was convinced," he later said of the judges. Swedish accounts say "naive" was a recurring verdict and that Marcus Wallenberg told them the banks would handle this themselves. Kreditor ranked last of three, a blow Siemiatkowski called "emotional".

The founders knew the safe path was close by. Siemiatkowski told the Swedish magazine Resultat in 2014 that they were weighing the company against a conventional career in banking and finance, when starting a business meant long weeks without pay. They shrank the risk with a deadline: six months, so that failure would cost half a year and a line on their CVs. They worked from seven in the morning until eleven at night, he said. His own response to the jury, he recalled, was "to curl up my fist and say 'I'll show you'."

An angel investor, Jane Walerud, agreed to put in about 600,000 kronor for 10 per cent; the money paid engineers to build the first system. The founders then drove around Sweden in an old Volvo, signing up small online shops one by one. Kreditor was renamed Klarna in 2009. Years later Siemiatkowski said "people were always telling me it wouldn't work."

quote.text: Till a man has declared his mind, his virtue and vice may have lain hidden; do not conclude that the thicket is unoccupied, peradventure the tiger is gone asleep
quote.locator: Chapter I, "Of the Customs of Kings", Story III
quote.source_title: The Persian Literature, Volume 2 (The Gulistan, tr. James Ross), Project Gutenberg eBook #13060
quote.connection: The jury judged slides from three students who had not yet done anything. Saadi's point is that worth stays hidden until it is acted on, which cuts both ways: the judges could not see what Kreditor would become, and neither could its founders. Their six months were a way of finding out.

reflection: An early verdict from people with standing can sit in you for years. It helps to remember what such a verdict is made of: a short look at an idea before anything has been tried. It says something about the slides, and very little about what you will do next.

What the founders did well was not only refuse the verdict. They turned it into a test with an end date and a known cost, so that neither the jury's doubt nor their own defiance had to settle the matter. Six months of work would.
invitation: If someone's early judgement of your work is still with you, write down one thing that would show, within a set time, whether they were right. Then choose the date and put it in your diary.

research_notes: As the brief asked, the setback is told on the founders' own account: the Sequoia profile (2023) and Siemiatkowski's 2014 interview with Resultat. Year: Resultat and Quartr say 2005; EFN (2025) places the pitch at the school's 'partnerstämma' in 2004 and Walerud's deal at the school's Christmas reception that year, so the story says '2004 or 2005' and approx_date is 2005, the founding year. Jury: Sequoia names Stefan Persson and 'a member of the Wallenberg family' and says the king attended; Resultat names Persson, Peggy Bruzelius and Investor's Marcus Wallenberg; EFN names Marcus Wallenberg (as SEB chairman), Bruzelius, Lars Pettersson and Claes Ekström and does not mention Persson. The story names only Persson and a Wallenberg, on Siemiatkowski's account, and attributes the Wallenberg remark to Swedish accounts. Placing: Sequoia says last of three; EFN and Resultat say last or unanimously panned; WebProNews (not cited) wrongly says they won. Walerud's stake: EFN quotes her as saying 600,000 kronor for 10 per cent; Sequoia says $60,000 for 10 per cent; at 2005 exchange rates 600,000 kronor was nearer $80,000, so the story uses her kronor figure. 'Naive', the career dilemma, the six-month deadline and the 07.00-23.00 schedule are paraphrased from the Swedish Resultat interview rather than quoted, to avoid presenting a translation as an exact quotation; the only direct quotations are from English sources. Sequoia orders events loosely (it calls the competition a setback 'just as the company was getting off the ground'); the story does not claim whether Walerud committed before or after the contest. Funding is 'mixed': a small angel stake, then a business that Siemiatkowski says was profitable for years, then venture capital from 2010. The Resultat page is partly paywalled but the cited passages load.
